title: Bound shopping text using Qt built-in fitting
severity_basis: Agent assessment: typography/readability defect, without observed data loss or blocked shopping actions.
scope: User requested removing the extra C++ scaler and relying on Text.Fit with a large default font. They then relaxed the two-line limit; three was recommended as a practical cap.
environment: Qt 6.12 MSVC Windows native rendering and Android 16/API 36 QShopper_API_36 emulator-5580 with host GPU rendering. User confirmed the desktop appearance and accepted closure; no physical-phone confirmation is claimed.
reproduction_status: Original native Windows preview renders four lines in some long-entry cases. The tested Android configuration renders at most three already; Android checks are controls for the relaxed three-line policy.
reproduction: Use a long unbroken or oversized multiword entry in a 9.27 mm row.
In the native Windows preview at scale 2, the original eight-line limit permits four lines.
actual: The original maximumLineCount of eight permits more lines than needed.
expected: Use Qt Text.Fit, the existing 7 mm default font and a three-line cap in the 9.27 mm row. Qt handles wrapping, shrinking and existing ellipsis. Keep saved names intact.
source_notes: The user rejected the additional font scaler as unnecessary complexity. Both C++ files and their CMake registration were removed.
The production change is maximumLineCount: 8 to 3. Text.Fit, 7 mm font, alignment, wrapping and right ellipsis remain as before.
The earlier strict two-line/full-content requirement is superseded. Tests allow Qt to elide long text instead of imposing a separate fitting algorithm.
Offscreen may expose only a dummy/icon font; actual-font checks also run with native Windows rendering. Android screenshot bands check actual visible line counts, not accessibility source labels.
acceptance_criteria: At most three rendered lines, with a large short-name font and fixed row height.
Use Qt built-in fitting and ellipsis; no additional font scaler.
Preserve checked styling, row reuse, resize behavior and complete stored names.
Demonstrate a failing-before/passing-after regression for the three-line cap and run Windows plus Android controls.
User acceptance of appearance before closure. Desktop confirmation was accepted for closure on 2026-10-31.

implementation.change: Set maximumLineCount to 3 in TextItem.qml, retaining Text.Fit and the existing 7 mm font. No additional scaler is used.
regression_tests: tests/qml/tst_textfitting.qml: 30 cases across five entry types, three widths and two scales, plus resize and two lifecycle records; 33 total.
tests/android/test_textfitting.py: 20 screenshot, font-size, palette and saved-text checks in Light/Dark.
implementation.windows_before: Native Windows original eight-line component: four of 33 records fail because long/unbroken inputs occupy four lines. The original component was rebuilt for the comparison, then the three-line source restored and rebuilt.
implementation.windows_after: All 33 focused native Windows records pass. The final configure/build/CTest workflow passes 148 UI, 6 keyboard and 61 model records (UI 173.50 seconds; total 179.74 seconds).
implementation.android_before: Original Android captures show three lines for extreme inputs, already within the relaxed three-line cap. These are platform controls, not a claimed Android reproduction of a four-line defect.
implementation.android_after: All 20 checks pass on the final Qt-native x86_64 APK in Light and Dark. Actual screenshot text bands, large short names, shrinking long text and complete stored names/flags are checked. Screenshots inspected.
implementation.isolation: UI harness uses in-memory SQLite and temporary settings; native tests only target emulator-5580 with unique data/settings and stop the app afterward.
implementation.history: Earlier UI-003 scaler/two-line reports are superseded. Final Qt-native reports use ui003-nativeqt paths.
implementation.remaining: None for closure. The user accepted desktop verification and requested marking the ticket fixed and committing; this supersedes the earlier phone-acceptance step.
